claims.statement: BidPoint is an early-scaffolding organization-level monorepo whose product delivery architecture is documented but whose concrete product implementations, per-module ownership rules, and product CI/CD workflows are not yet implemented; the OpenWiki updater is documentation automation rather than a product pipeline.
Every committed artifact is intended to have exactly one owning module, while a pull request may coordinate multiple modules only when it explains why the change must cross their boundaries.

The pull request template asks authors to identify affected modules, confirm one owner per artifact, justify cross-module work, avoid committed secrets and environment-specific values, update a module README when responsibilities change, and add an ADR for architectural decisions.
CODEOWNERS currently contains only a repository-wide wildcard owned by @LaNguAx; per-module ownership rules have not been added.

Significant architectural choices must be recorded under docs/adr with their context and rejected alternatives, while routine implementation of an already-decided design does not become an architectural decision merely because it coordinates modules.

Product workflows are intended to be path-scoped so unrelated domains do not trigger one another, and a job that must consume paths from multiple domains for one responsibility is a signal that the boundary may be wrong.

Web and mobile are intended as independent workspace roots with separate toolchains, dependency graphs, and CI paths rather than a shared frontend build root, but none of those concrete mechanisms exists yet.

The intended backend CI boundary is to build, test, and publish container artifacts to ECR; backend source does not own deployment infrastructure, and gitops owns how the published images are deployed and scaled.

Git is intended to be the source of truth for Kubernetes desired state in gitops, and a GitOps controller such as ArgoCD reconciles the cluster toward that state; gitops assumes the cluster already exists and does not provision infrastructure.

For cluster workloads, CI is intended to publish an artifact and change the image version in GitOps state, after which the controller reconciles the cluster; CI must not deploy cluster workloads directly.

Direct CI delivery is limited to non-cluster artifacts: mobile store releases and a static web bundle if static hosting is selected; if web is deployed as a cluster workload, it must use the GitOps path.

Mobile build, signing, and store-release configuration belongs with the mobile client because it is inseparable from its toolchain, while the workflow that executes the release belongs under .github; mobile releases also have a store-review gate and must not contain committed credentials.

The web deployment model is intentionally undecided between static hosting and a server runtime, so application code must not encode either assumption and the eventual selection must be recorded in an ADR.

Infrastructure definitions belong in infra while .github workflows only validate and apply them; infrastructure changes have a slower, stateful, harder-to-reverse risk profile than workload changes and must remain separate from GitOps workload reconciliation.
Concrete Infrastructure as Code and infrastructure workflows are absent; Terraform or OpenTofu is only a likely future mechanism rather than a currently selected implementation.

Backend behavior configuration is intended to be served by a configuration server and consumed at startup or on refresh, allowing behavior changes without rebuilding or redeploying the workload, but no configuration sets or configuration server are implemented.
dev, staging, and prod are separate environments, and a change intended for one must not implicitly alter another.

Secret values must never be committed: credentials live in an external secret manager, while Git may contain only references; workflow secret names and expressions such as GitHub secrets references identify credential sources but are not credential values.

The implemented OpenWiki workflow can be started manually or by the daily cron schedule 0 8 * * *, runs on ubuntu-latest, and has contents and pull-requests write permissions for creating its update branch and pull request.

The OpenWiki workflow checks out the repository with full history because openwiki code --update diffs HEAD against the last documented commit and a shallow clone can hide that commit and yield an empty change summary.
The OpenWiki workflow uses SHA-pinned checkout and Node setup actions, Node.js 22, exact global versions openwiki@0.4.3, mermaid@11.16.0, and jsdom@29.1.1, then runs openwiki code --update --print.

The OpenWiki run maps OPENWIKI_LANGSMITH_API_KEY and LANGSMITH_API_KEY to GitHub secret references, documents the former for authenticated LangSmith code-mode pull and the latter as optional tracing authentication, and notes that browser-login authentication for the selected OpenAI provider has no unattended equivalent.

After OpenWiki runs, the SHA-pinned create-pull-request action proposes only openwiki, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and the OpenWiki workflow itself on branch openwiki/update, using docs: update OpenWiki as the commit message and pull request title.
